# Diagnosing the Single LED Brake Light Failure on a 2015 Kia Sedona

When the brake pedal is depressed on your 2015 Kia Sedona and only the high-mounted center stop lamp illuminates while the two lower taillights remain dark, the issue is rarely a simple bulb failure or a blown fuse. Your initial diagnostics have already ruled out the most common culprits: the brake light switch appears functional because the center LED activates, the main fuse is intact (evidenced by the engine control module refusing to crank without it), and the rear light sockets are receiving power since all other running lights function correctly. This leaves us with a specific failure mode where the signal to ground is being completed for the center lamp but not for the lower pair.

In automotive electrical architecture, the brake lights operate on a switched ground circuit controlled by the pedal assembly. When you press the pedal, the switch closes, connecting the battery voltage from the fuse box to the common positive rail of the rear light cluster. The bulbs or LEDs then provide the path to ground through their internal filaments or semiconductor junctions. If only the center unit lights up, the power source and the primary switching mechanism are confirmed working. The isolation of the lower pair suggests a fault located specifically within the vehicle's body control module (BCM) logic, a harness interruption, or a localized short in the wiring loom that bypasses the lower LEDs.

Consider the possibility of a compromised wiring harness between the BCM and the rear light assembly. In many minivans, the rear lighting circuit runs through tight bends near the suspension components or inside the wheel wells. If there is an existing crack in the insulation on the wire leading to the lower brake lights, pressing the pedal might create a momentary connection that powers the center LED if the BCM logic prioritizes certain circuits, or more likely, the voltage is being siphoned off by a short before it can reach the lower sockets. This manifests as a "ghost load" where the current takes the path of least resistance through a damaged wire rather than through the intended light bulbs.

Another potential cause is an internal fault within the rear lamp assembly itself that isn't immediately visible upon visual inspection. The socket for the center high-mounted stop lamp might be physically distinct from the sockets for the lower taillights, perhaps using a different connector or having a separate ground strap. If the ground strap for the entire cluster is loose or corroded at the chassis connection point, but the center LED has its own dedicated ground path (which is rare but possible in some designs), you would see this specific behavior. However, it is more probable that the lower pair shares a common ground that is compromised, preventing them from completing the circuit even though they receive the switched positive voltage.

It is also worth investigating whether a diagnostic mode or a software configuration has inadvertently been altered. While accidental setting changes are possible in modern Kias, they rarely result in a hardware-specific isolation like this unless a calibration reset occurred after a battery disconnect or a repair attempt. If you have performed any recent maintenance involving the rear bumper or undercarriage, check for pinch points where the wiring harness could have been damaged.

To confirm the wiring integrity, you would need to perform a voltage drop test on the lower brake light circuits with the pedal depressed. Measure the voltage at the connector leading to the lower lights relative to chassis ground. If you read full battery voltage (approx 12V+), the issue is almost certainly an open circuit in the bulb socket or the bulb itself, despite your initial assumption that the socket isn't broken. If you read significantly less than 12V, there is a high-resistance connection or a partial short in the wiring harness between the rear assembly and the front of the vehicle.
